NijRAW · Help
Everything stays on your device

The name: Nij (निज) is Sanskrit for "one's own," a nod to the idea that your photos and their data never leave your device and remain entirely yours.

The demo opens on YouTube in a new browser tab. Everything else in NijRAW stays on your device, and nothing is uploaded.

New here? A 60-second walkthrough

1
For best compatibility, use an up-to-date browser with standard privacy settings. Tap Import (top-left) and choose a photo, JPEG, PNG, or a camera RAW. It loads instantly at preview quality, and your full-resolution file is used when you export.
2
Tap Auto in the action bar for a one-tap improvement, then nudge the sliders in the panels on the right (or the bottom sheet on mobile), Exposure, Contrast, Temperature are the ones to start with.
3
Want the person to pop from the background? Open the Subject tab and tap Auto-Detect Subject, then brighten the Subject layer or darken the Background.
4
Clean up skin in the Retouch tab (Heal / Smooth / Eyes), and reduce grain with Denoise in the action bar.
5
Tap Split compare in the action bar to slide a divider across the photo and check your edit against the original. When you are happy with it, tap Export and pick a format, JPEG, PNG, or modern WebP / AVIF where your browser supports them, choose sRGB or Display P3 colour, and pick a size: Original, 4K, web, or a social-ready 1080 px long edge. It saves straight to your device.

That is the whole loop. Nothing is uploaded, and your work is saved in the browser automatically, so you can close the tab and come back to it. For step-by-step detail, see How to use.

The action bar, button by button

On phones these show as icons only. Here is what each one does:

Undo / Redo: the left arrow steps backward (Ctrl/⌘+Z); the right arrow steps forward (Ctrl/⌘+Shift+Z). Up to 60 steps.
Crop: drag handles to reframe; pick an aspect ratio (1:1, 16:9, 4:3…) or Free.
Rotate: opens rotate & straighten: 90° turns, flips, and a fine angle slider.
Auto: one-tap tone, colour and white-balance correction, with a Portrait/Landscape override and an intensity slider.
Denoise: variance-stabilised, structure-aware noise reduction. Tap Auto to set an amount from the photo's own noise, or drag the strength slider; it keeps detail while removing grain.
Split compare: drags a divider across the photo, original on one side, your edit on the other. Slide it to inspect any area. Tap again to turn off.
Hold to compare: press and hold the eye button (or the \ key) to flash the untouched original; release to return to your edit. The quickest before/after there is.
Photo Assistant: at the top of the Quick tab. It measures your photo (exposure, clipping, colour cast, flat tones, tilted horizon, noise) and offers up to five plain-language one-tap fixes, each explaining why. Tap to apply, tap again to undo just that fix, or Fix everything above. Tap Re-analyse after big changes, since it always measures your current edit. Its first row is Auto enhance, the same engine as the top-bar Auto button, applied reversibly; once it runs, the assistant re-measures, so the remaining fixes are only what Auto left behind.
Histogram point: tap to cycle Black-point → White-point → Off, then click on a histogram to set that tonal anchor from the image itself.
History: opens a panel listing every edit step. Click any step to jump straight back to it.
Reset All: clears every adjustment and returns to the imported photo. Your original is never altered.

The Import, theme, help, and Export buttons live in the very top bar above this one.

Everything stays on your device

1 · Open a photo

Tap Import in the top bar and choose a JPEG, PNG, or RAW file (ARW, NEF, CR2, CR3, DNG and more). Large images are previewed at reduced size for speed; export always renders at full resolution.

2 · Make global adjustments

Use the panels on the right (or the bottom sheet on mobile) for exposure, colour, tone curves, detail, effects, and crop. Tap Auto in the action bar for a one-tap starting point, and pick Portrait or Landscape if it guesses wrong.

3 · Isolate the subject

Open the Subject tab and tap Auto-Detect Subject. If detection misses, Brush roughly over the subject or draw a region, then fine-tune with the Detection tuning sliders. Once a mask exists, the Subject and Background layers can be edited separately.

4 · Retouch skin & eyes

  1. Open the Retouch tab.
  2. Pick a tool: Heal (remove blemishes), Smooth (soften skin), or Eyes (brighten). The brush turns on automatically.
  3. Tap a spot or drag over an area directly on the photo.
  4. Adjust Size and Strength; use Undo last or Clear all as needed.

Prefer one tap? Auto Improve softens skin across the whole frame at a gentle strength.

5 · Crop & straighten

Tap the Crop tool in the action bar, drag the handles to frame your shot, and pick an aspect ratio from the bar at the bottom: 1:1, 16:9, 9:16, 4:3 and more. Free removes the constraint. Rotate and straighten live in the Crop & Rotate panel. Once you have applied a crop, a Reset size chip appears at the end of that same bar; tap it to restore the photo's original dimensions while keeping every other edit you have made since, then reframe from the full frame if you want a different crop.

6 · Reduce noise

Tap Denoise in the action bar and tap Auto to let NijRAW estimate a suitable amount from the photo's own noise, or drag the strength slider to set it yourself. The edge-aware filter cleans grain while keeping detail, and computes in the background so the app stays responsive (the preview updates a moment after you let go).

7 · Export

Tap Export and choose a format: JPEG, PNG, or, where your browser supports them, WebP and AVIF (smaller files at the same quality). Set the Quality and pick a Colour space (sRGB for everywhere, Display P3 for wide-gamut). Uncheck Include metadata first if you do not want the camera's EXIF/GPS data (make, model, lens, ISO, capture time, location, and so on) carried into the exported file; see the next step for details. The file saves straight to your device, and nothing is uploaded.

8 · Save as a project file (.nijraw)

A .nijraw file is NijRAW's own project format for photo edits: one file holding your untouched original photo plus every adjustment, mask and crop, still fully editable.

  1. Tap Export, then under Keep everything editable tap Save project (.nijraw).
  2. The file downloads as yourphoto.nijraw straight to your device, and nothing is uploaded.
  3. To keep working on it later, tap Import (or drag the file in) and pick that .nijraw file like any photo. It reopens with every edit exactly as you left it, ready to continue.

This is different from a rendered export (JPEG/PNG/TIFF/WebP/AVIF), which bakes your edit into a fixed image. Save a .nijraw file whenever you might want to keep adjusting later, and export a rendered format when you are ready to share or print.

9 · Choosing whether to keep metadata on export

The export popover has an Include metadata checkbox, on by default. With it checked, the camera's EXIF/GPS data captured on import, make, model, lens, ISO, shutter speed, aperture, capture time, and location if the photo has it, is written back into JPEG, WebP, and TIFF (both 8-bit and 16-bit) exports. Uncheck it before exporting to strip that metadata from the file instead, for example before sharing a photo publicly. The choice applies per export, so double-check the box each time if you want a different result than last time. (PNG and AVIF exports do not currently carry this metadata either way.)

10 · Local adjustments (Subject tab)

Open Local adjustments in the Subject tab and pick a mask type: Radial (elliptical spotlight), Linear (graduated fade), Brush (paint freehand), or Auto (drag a box and the standout surface inside it is selected for you, then touched up with its own Erase/Add brushes). The mask appears on the photo with draggable handles. Each mask carries its own Light (exposure, brightness, contrast) and Colour (saturation, temperature, tint, hue) sliders plus a master Strength control that scales the whole effect, and every mask can be inverted, duplicated, reset, hidden with the eye toggle, or deleted from the list. Masks stack in order, so you can dodge, burn and colour-shift several regions independently.

11 · Looks, LUTs & recipes

  1. In the Advanced tab, open Looks & LUT.
  2. Save current look stores your whole edit as a reusable tile.
  3. Load .cube LUT applies a 3D colour grade; adjust its Intensity or remove it.
  4. From the Export menu, Save recipe writes a portable .json you can share or re-apply later with Load recipe.

12 · Apply an edit to many photos (batch)

Edit one photo the way you want, then open Export → Apply edit to many photos and select several files. The adjustments you made to the open photo are applied to each selected photo, and an edited copy of every one is saved to your device, all in one pass, and nothing is uploaded. (It copies adjustments like exposure, colour and tone; per-photo work such as crop and retouch is not carried over.)

13 · Clone & patch

In the Retouch tab choose Clone. Tap once to set a source, then paint elsewhere to copy that area over, colour-matched so it blends. Tap Set new source to re-pick.

14 · Library, keep & organise your photos

Tap Library in the top bar to open your on-device catalogue. Photos you open are added automatically; use Add photos to bring in more (including RAW, HEIC and standard formats). Each tile tracks your latest edit, and your adjustments auto-save as you work, so reopening a photo lands exactly where you left off, and a RAW even re-runs its full sensor decode from the original bytes.

  1. Rate and flag: give each photo 0–5 stars and mark it a pick or reject to sort the keepers from the culls.
  2. Filter and sort: the bar at the top filters by minimum rating, flag, or album, and sorts by date added, capture date, recently edited, rating or name. The search box matches name, camera and lens.
  3. Albums: select photos and use Album… to add them to a new or existing album, then filter to it.
  4. Export selected: renders each chosen photo with its own saved edits in one pass, straight to your device.
  5. Remove takes photos out of the catalogue. Everything stays in your browser, nothing is uploaded, and a storage readout shows how much space the library uses.

Zoom & pan

A + / − control sits in the corner of the photo; tap to zoom in or out, or tap the percentage between them to reset to 100%. You can also scroll to zoom on desktop, or pinch with two fingers on touch. A hand button next to it toggles Pan mode; with it on, drag directly on the photo (mouse or one finger) to move around, and double-tap resets the view. Pan is off by default so a normal drag never shifts the photo, and it does not interfere with tools that use the photo directly, like the brush, retouch, crop, or subject tap-to-focus.

Photo Insights: learn from each shot

The Insights tab gives concise, cited feedback on a photo. First answer two quick things it cannot reliably guess: where the subject is (drag a box around it on the photo, which also tells the app how much of the frame it fills) and, optionally, what kind of shot it is (it can infer portrait vs landscape from how much the subject covers) and which way it faces. You can also tell it whether the photo was taken on a phone or a camera (it pre-fills this from the photo's metadata), since phones have far less dynamic range, so blown highlights and crushed shadows are judged more leniently for a phone and more strictly for a camera that had the latitude to avoid them. From there it computes the rest from the pixels: rule-of-thirds placement and active space, subject size and how it separates from the background, background clutter, horizon level and placement, depth/foreground, frame orientation, exposure (highlight/shadow clipping and tonal range), lighting direction and quality, colour balance and saturation, and overall focus. It also reads the tones numerically: the tonal range you occupy expressed in Ansel Adams' Zones (0–IX), exactly how much clipping is present as a percentage of pixels (with a note on when clipping is fine, like specular glints), where the mass of your histogram sits (low-key, high-key or balanced), and your global contrast. Once you start editing, an extra "Your edit · measured change" panel appears showing how your adjustments moved those same numbers, tonal range widened, highlights recovered, contrast added, so you can connect the slider you moved to the measured result. Each point comes with a short lesson and a reference (e.g. Freeman's The Photographer's Eye, Adams' Zone System, Hunter's Light: Science & Magic) so you can look it up and shoot better next time. Composition uses your answers; everything else is measured on your device, and nothing is uploaded. Treat it as guidance, not gospel.

RAW developing

Reads embedded full-size previews and raw sensor data from RAW files and gives full tone control: exposure, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, curves, white balance, HSL, colour grading, clarity, dehaze, sharpening, noise reduction, edge-aware denoise, vignette and grain.

Subject isolation

Automatic subject detection with brush and region guidance, plus advanced sliders (Saliency, Detail, Sensitivity, BG Pinning, Edge Snap) and a manual mask touch-up brush. Subject and background become independent editing layers.

Cleaning up a subject mask

After detection the Subject tab offers a row of fix-ups for an imperfect mask. Remove dendrites drops loose specks and thin strays, keeping the main connected bodies (so split subjects survive). Shrink edge pulls the whole mask boundary inward by one pixel per tap; tap it a few times to peel off a thin background fringe, such as sky haloing the subject. Erase mask opens the touch-up controls: paint with your finger to remove mask (or switch to Add to paint mask back), adjust the brush with Size, and step back with Undo. While erasing, Cut colour changes a tap into a colour flood; it lifts a fused leak (e.g. a wall blob touching a head) by clearing the connected patch of similar colour, with the Size slider widening the colour tolerance. The match is texture-aware: it compares local colour averages with a tolerance that adapts to the tapped surface's own variation, so it works on grass, gravel and foliage as well as flat walls and sky. Add Everywhere to clear that tapped colour from every gap at once, ideal for sky showing through several openings between two people. Add and Cut colour are opposite modes, so turning one on switches the other off.

Geometric masks

Build a mask from a linear gradient or radial shape in the Subject tab, then drag its handles directly on the photo to move, rotate, scale, and set feather. The masked area becomes the Subject layer and everything else the Background, so the two can be graded independently, ideal for skies, vignettes, and spotlighting.

Local adjustments (stackable masks)

Beyond the single subject mask, add as many radial, linear, brush, and region-based auto masks as you like (an auto mask selects the similar surface inside a box you drag, and can be refined with its Erase/Add brushes), each with its own exposure, contrast, saturation, temperature, tint and hue. Place them directly on the photo, invert any of them, and toggle or remove individual masks from a list. They stack in order, so you can dodge, burn, and colour-shift different regions independently.

Looks, LUTs & recipes

Save any edit as a reusable look, or load an industry-standard .cube 3D LUT for a cinematic grade with an adjustable intensity. Export a portable .json recipe of all your adjustments to share or re-apply to other photos later.

Apply an edit to many photos (batch)

Take the adjustments on your open photo and apply them to a whole set of other photos at once, each is saved as an edited copy. Works with RAW, HEIC and standard formats, without anything leaving your device.

Clone & patch

A content-aware Clone tool: pick a source point and paint elsewhere to copy that area over, colour-matched to blend seamlessly, for removing larger objects that Heal's automatic donor cannot cover.

Export formats & colour management

Export JPEG, PNG, TIFF (8-bit or 16-bit), and modern WebP / AVIF (smaller files at the same quality, where supported). Choose sRGB or Display P3. Open HEIC/HEIF photos from modern phones too. An Include metadata checkbox in the export popover controls whether the camera's EXIF/GPS data is written into JPEG, WebP, and TIFF exports; leave it checked to keep make, model, lens, ISO and capture details, or uncheck it to strip that metadata before sharing.

Project files (.nijraw)

Beyond rendered exports, Save project (.nijraw) writes your untouched original photo plus every edit, mask and adjustment into a single portable file. Reopen a .nijraw file with Import any time to keep editing exactly where you left off, without re-decoding or losing any adjustment.

Compare & history

A draggable split-compare slider shows original and edit side by side, a clickable histogram lets you set black and white points from the image, and an edit-history panel lists every step so you can jump straight back to any point.

Reset crop size

Once you have applied at least one crop to a photo, the crop tool's aspect-ratio bar gains a Reset size chip. It restores the photo's pre-crop dimensions while leaving every other adjustment, tone, colour, curves, retouch, masks, exactly as it was, so you can start a fresh crop from the full frame without losing anything else you have done. It works no matter how many crops or other edits happened since; the one exception is Bake & auto-crop's geometry correction, which replaces the pre-crop reference the same way a new photo would.

Library & catalogue

A persistent, on-device Library keeps your photos, edits and organisation between sessions. Rate photos 0–5 stars, mark picks and rejects, group them into albums, and filter or sort by rating, flag, album, capture date or recently edited, or search by name, camera and lens. Each photo stores its original file bytes plus your full edit state, so reopening one restores everything (and re-decodes RAW from source). Export selected renders every chosen photo with its own saved edits at once. It is a normal catalogue workflow, entirely in your browser, and nothing is uploaded.

Denoise: Hybrid pipeline

A robust denoiser reachable from the Denoise shortcut in the action bar. It stabilises the camera's signal-dependent noise, then measures the remaining local noise covariance rather than assuming it, matches similar patches by Mahalanobis distance (the true statistical distance under that covariance) with a gate that admits only differences noise can explain, adapts patch size to local structure (small on edges, large in smooth areas), suppresses the random component with low-rank shrinkage across a Gaussian/Laplacian pyramid, treats coarse chroma (colour-blotch) noise on two dedicated coarse scales, and blends by a per-pixel confidence map, so only statistically probable sensor noise is removed while texture, edges and fine detail stay crisp. Runs off the main thread so the interface stays responsive.

The pop-out has two sliders. Strength is the main control: it switches denoising on and sets how hard the luminance (detail/grain) chain works, ramping gently so texture stays protected even at high values, and at 0, denoising is off entirely. Colour is independent of Strength and governs only the chroma (colour-blotch) chain: it controls how aggressively mottled colour noise is merged and flattened across the coarse and fine chroma bands, separately from luminance detail. It defaults to 100, which cleans colour speckling fully without softening the image, since smoothing chroma costs little sharpness; lower it if you want to preserve fine colour variation, such as freckles or subtle colour texture, that full chroma cleanup would flatten.

Clipping warning

Toggle Show clipping in the Histogram panel (or press J) to highlight blown highlights in red and crushed shadows in blue, so you can pull back exposure before losing detail. The warning is preview-only, it is never baked into your export.

Defringe

Removes purple and green chromatic-aberration fringes along high-contrast edges (common in backlit shots) while preserving luminance, so edges stay sharp and only the false colour is suppressed.

Edge-aware sharpening (Sharpen Mask)

Sharpening uses a modern halo-free chain instead of classic unsharp masking: it works on luminance only (colour noise and fringes are never amplified), separates detail from structure with an edge-preserving guided filter (so no bright/dark halos ring around edges), passes every detail coefficient through a noise gate calibrated to the photo's own measured noise floor (real texture is boosted fully, noise-scale wiggles barely at all), and finally applies an overshoot clamp that makes residual ringing impossible while still letting fine texture gain contrast. The Sharpen Mask slider sets the strength of the noise gate: at 0 a mild gate still protects grain; at 100 flat areas (skies, skin, out-of-focus background) are almost untouched while edges and texture get the full effect.

Lens corrections

The Lens Corrections panel fixes two common optical defects. Distortion straightens bowed lines: positive values correct barrel (bulging) distortion, negative values correct pincushion (pinched) distortion. A small automatic zoom keeps the corrected image filling the frame with no visible gaps at the corners, so you never see blank wedges from the correction itself. Vignetting evens out corner brightness: positive brightens corners darkened by optical fall-off, negative deepens them for a stylised look; this is independent of the separate, purely cosmetic Vignette in the Effects panel. If the photo's EXIF data names a lens we recognise, sensible Distortion and Vignetting starting values for that lens are applied automatically the first time the photo loads. You are told which lens was detected, and can fine-tune or fully override the result with the sliders at any time. You can also pick a make and model yourself from the dropdowns above the sliders, whether or not EXIF data is present, to load that lens's starting values on demand.

Luminance histogram

A Luminance toggle in the Histogram panel overlays a perceptual-brightness curve on top of the red, green and blue channels, so you can read overall tonal distribution, where shadows, midtones and highlights sit, separately from individual colour channels.

Settings search

The search box at the top of the Advanced panel filters every setting as you type. Match a section name (e.g. "Light") or any individual control (e.g. "Defringe"); matching sections expand automatically. Clear the box to restore the panel exactly as it was.

Per-section reset

Each adjustment section header has a small reset (↺) control that reverts just that group of sliders to their defaults in a single undoable step, so you can start over on, say, Colour Grading without disturbing the rest of your edit.

Perspective correction

One tap of Auto-straighten horizon (in the Rotate menu) finds the horizon line and levels it. Vertical and horizontal keystone sliders in the Geometry panel straighten converging lines, leaning buildings, tilted architecture, with a true projective warp. Use Bake & auto-crop to apply the correction and automatically trim the exposed edges to the largest clean rectangle.

Copy & paste edits

Found a look you like? Copy edit (top of the Advanced panel, or Ctrl/⌘+Shift+C) captures all your adjustments, colour, curves, HSL and grading; open another photo and Paste edit (Ctrl/⌘+Shift+V) applies the same look instantly. Photo-specific work, masks, retouch, crop, stays with each image.

Retouch

Content-aware Heal that samples clean skin nearby, frequency-separation Smooth that keeps pores, and an Eyes tool for brightening, all non-destructive and undoable.

Auto enhance

One-tap tone, colour and white-balance correction that adapts to the image, with a manual Portrait/Landscape override and an intensity that stays natural.

Non-destructive workflow

Up to 60 steps of undo/redo, before/after compare, presets, and crop & straighten; your original is never altered.

Workspace memory

Your photo and every adjustment are saved locally in the browser as you work, so closing the tab or refreshing the page brings the session right back. Your full undo/redo history is saved too, not just the latest state, so if you left mid-edit, or came back later to keep going, Undo and Redo still step through the same edits you made before you left. If the photo was a RAW opened with a true sensor decode, revisiting it shows an honest Sensor render · 8-bit chip (the 16-bit master itself is too large to keep between visits) and quietly re-decodes the sensor data in the background, restoring Sensor · 16-bit with all your edits and history carried over. Nothing leaves your device; the workspace is stored in your own browser, not on any server.

Private by design

The entire editor runs in your browser. Every file you open, JPEG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, HEIC, or any camera RAW, is treated the same way: it is read and processed only on your device and is never uploaded anywhere. The same is true of everything the app produces: exports, recipes, batch copies, the library, and your saved workspace all stay on this device. No uploads, no accounts, no tracking.

On-device processing

Every pixel operation runs locally in JavaScript on a canvas. For responsiveness, edits preview on a downscaled proxy; on export the same operations replay against the full-resolution image.

True RAW decoding (LibRaw, WebAssembly)

When the RAW engine is available and auto-decode is on (the default), opening a RAW goes straight to the true sensor master: a full LibRaw 0.21 engine, compiled to WebAssembly and embedded in this page, running in a one-shot Web Worker, decodes the actual sensor mosaic before you start editing. That means real demosaic (AHD by default, DHT/VNG/bilinear selectable), the camera's as-shot white balance, and LibRaw's per-camera colour matrix, rendered to 16-bit RGB, are the very first pixels you touch. There is no 8-bit preview to edit first and no preview→sensor hand-off partway through. Before any tone mapping, an automatic scene-referred highlight reconstruction stage rebuilds channels the sensor clipped from the ones that survived, using the colour of the unclipped surroundings, and rolls the recovered light back under white with a smooth shoulder, so blown skies and bright edges keep natural colour instead of going flat white or magenta. It needs no settings, only touches near-clipped pixels, and skips itself entirely when the frame has no clipping. Decode progress shows live on the provenance chip in the top bar (a few seconds for a full-resolution frame). The camera's embedded JPEG preview remains the graceful fallback: if the engine is unavailable in your browser, you have turned auto-decode off, or the sensor decode fails, the preview opens instantly and the sensor decode is offered (or retried) in the background instead. The chip always states exactly which pixels you are editing, Sensor · 16-bit or Embedded preview · 8-bit, and opens the demosaic, white-balance, highlight and resolution settings. Nothing is fetched or compiled remotely.

The 16-bit master is memory-only and is not written to the workspace save (it is too large, tens to hundreds of MB per photo). Revisiting a RAW session, after a reload, or reopening a photo you left mid-edit, restores the 8-bit render that decode produced, labelled honestly as Sensor render · 8-bit rather than mis-stated as a fresh preview fallback, then re-attaches the original file bytes from the Library and quietly re-runs the sensor decode in the background. When it lands, the chip returns to Sensor · 16-bit and every edit, including the full undo/redo history, is re-pointed onto the newly decoded buffers rather than lost, so the session picks up exactly where it left off. This auto re-decode only fires when the working image is still the untouched full sensor frame; if you had cropped or run Bake & auto-crop since the original decode, re-adopting the full frame would silently undo that, so the chip stays on the restored render and offers a manual re-decode instead.

The 16-bit pipeline

The decoded 16-bit frame is kept as a master for the life of the photo (crops and geometry bakes are applied to it in parallel). Interactively, tone and curves are applied through a 65 536-entry LUT sampled from the same tone function as the preview path, reading the 16-bit data directly, so deep shadow lifts and steep curves draw on real sensor precision instead of re-quantised 8-bit values. Standard JPEG/PNG exports tone-map straight from the master too. Both TIFF · 16-bit and the ordinary TIFF command render the complete tonal, colour, retouch, detail and geometry pipeline: whenever a true 16-bit sensor master backs the photo and every active adjustment can be honoured in 16-bit, even a plain TIFF export is written at full 16-bit precision with an embedded ICC profile, rather than read back from the 8-bit canvas. If an adjustment the 16-bit path cannot reproduce is active (denoise, defringe, film grain, or layer/local masks) the plain TIFF falls back to the fully-rendered 8-bit canvas so nothing you see on screen is dropped; the explicit TIFF · 16-bit command lists any such omissions before export.

Reset crop size

The first time a crop is applied to a photo, its pre-crop pixel buffer, and, for a RAW, the matching 16-bit sensor master, is kept in memory as a snapshot; later crops do not overwrite it, so Reset size always returns to the true original dimensions in one step, however many crops followed. Only the pixel buffers are swapped back; every non-destructive parameter (exposure, colour, curves, HSL, effects, rotation and flips) lives separately and is untouched by the reset, so nothing else about your edit changes. The snapshot is invalidated (and the reset chip disappears) if you load a new photo, close the current one, or run Bake & auto-crop's geometry correction, since baking permanently changes what "original" means for that photo.

Library

The library is an on-device IndexedDB catalogue. Each entry stores the original file bytes verbatim (a CR2 stays a CR2 and re-runs the full sensor decode when reopened), a thumbnail that tracks your edit, the complete edit state including retouch and masks, and ratings/flags/keywords/albums. Edits auto-save to the catalogue as you work, so a photo reopened later lands exactly where you left it, and "Export selected" renders each photo with its own saved edits. Like everything else, it never leaves your device.

Session persistence & undo history

The open workspace (the auto-restored session, distinct from the Library catalogue) debounce-saves to IndexedDB on every committed edit: the current parameters, the proxy/original pixel Blobs, and the full undo/redo stack. History steps store only their lightweight parameters (sliders, curves, HSL, retouch ops, mask geometry), not pixel copies, since every step that shares the current pixel identity can be replayed against the one persisted original/proxy pair; subject masks are deduplicated by reference so a mask reused across many steps is encoded once. On restore, the stack is rebuilt and your position in it (including any pending redo) comes back exactly as you left it. Steps from a pixel identity the session no longer holds (the far side of a crop, a geometry bake, or, for RAW, a pre-adoption preview render) are pruned rather than restored broken, so the kept history always starts from a buffer that is actually still on disk. The RAW sensor-decode adoption step (see above) re-points any in-memory history at its freshly decoded buffers before that happens, precisely so a background re-decode after a revisit does not itself get treated as a break in identity and prune the history that was just restored.

Denoise: Hybrid pipeline

Denoising runs as an eight-stage mathematical chain, with no learned components. A Generalized Anscombe transform first stabilises variance: a Poisson–Gaussian noise model v(I) ≈ a·I + b is estimated from the flattest regions of the frame, and f(I) = (2/a)·√(a·I + ⅜a² + b) maps the camera's signal-dependent noise to approximately unit-variance Gaussian noise. Because demosaicing and model error leave that residual noise both spatially varying and pixel-correlated, the pipeline then measures the local noise covariance in the stabilised domain: a per-pixel variance map σ²(x,y) is fitted on a tile grid using only low-coherence (flat) pixels, and a lag-1 correlation ρ is estimated from horizontal pixel differences, giving Σ(x) = σ²(x)·R(ρ) with R an AR(1) correlation. Similar patches are then grouped by Mahalanobis distance, squared differences whitened through the AR(1) innovation filter and scaled by the local variance, i.e. dᵀΣ⁻¹d in O(patch) time, plus a structure-tensor penalty (gradient orientation and coherence), so groups agree in appearance and geometry under the true noise metric. A χ²-style gate exploits the fact that a noise-only match has a whitened per-coefficient distance of expectation 1: candidates beyond 1 + 3·√(2/PC) are rejected, so genuine texture, which differs by more than noise allows, never enters a group and cannot be averaged away. Patch size adapts to coherence: strongly oriented pixels use tight 3×3 patches that hug the edge, smooth regions use 7×7 patches for stronger averaging. Each group receives WNNM-style low-rank suppression: the group mean carries the coherent structure while per-coefficient deviations are shrunk with an empirical Wiener rule whose noise floor is the local σ²(x), eased where tensor coherence is high to protect edges, corners and directional texture. Grouping runs multi-scale over a Gaussian/Laplacian pyramid: luminance is additionally denoised on a half-resolution Gaussian level (own tensor field, variance propagated as σ²(1+ρ)²/4) and recombined through the Laplacian identity, so blotchy low-frequency noise beyond the full-res search window is removed while the full-resolution detail band passes through untouched; coarse chroma noise, intrinsically large-scale because demosaicing interpolates colour over several pixels, is grouped on two pyramid levels (half and quarter resolution, recombined through the Laplacian identity) with its own tensor fields and robust σ per level, while the pixel-level chroma band, which carries almost no real image colour, is suppressed directly with strength; the chroma blend is deliberately not throttled by the luminance confidence map, since colour blotches do not respect luma edges. Finally a per-pixel confidence map, local variance tested against the local noise floor σ²(x), gated by coherence, blends the result so strong denoising applies only where noise is statistically likely and high-confidence detail is left largely untouched. The Strength slider is t above, scaling the luminance chain and the overall denoised→original blend; the Colour slider is tC, scaling only the chroma-band range filters, the coarse/medium replacement mix and the fine chroma-speckle suppression described above, independently of luminance strength or confidence. It runs in a Web Worker off the main thread; on export the same pipeline is applied at full resolution in parallel strips.

Geometric masks

Gradient and radial masks are stored as vector control points in normalised image space, so they survive rotation, flip and zoom and rasterise cleanly at any resolution. A linear mask projects each pixel onto the gradient axis; a radial mask measures normalised distance inside an ellipse, both with an adjustable feathered falloff, and the result feeds the same Subject/Background layer engine as detected masks.

Local-adjustment masks

Each stackable local mask stores its geometry in normalised (0–1) image space and computes a per-pixel influence field with a smoothstep falloff: radial masks use an elliptical distance with a feather band, linear masks a clamped projection onto the gradient axis, and brush masks the union of soft circular stamps. Adjustments are applied weighted by that field and composited in order, so they map identically from the on-screen proxy to the full-resolution export.

LUTs & recipes

A loaded .cube file is parsed into a 3D colour table and applied as the final colour transform with trilinear interpolation between the nearest lattice points, blended toward the original by the intensity control. A recipe is the serialisable subset of your edit, global parameters, layer adjustments, wheels, curves, HSL and local masks, written as JSON; pixels, bitmap masks and crops stay with each image.

Edge-aware sharpening

Sharpening runs on luminance only, so chroma noise and colour fringes are never amplified. Rather than a Gaussian blur, the base (structure) layer is built with a self-guided edge-preserving filter: a local linear model is fit between the luminance and itself in a window of radius r (variance ε ≈ (18/255 of range)², so texture falls into the detail band while genuine strong edges are kept in the base), and the smoothed result carries no cross-edge overshoot the way a Gaussian base does, removing most halos at the source rather than clamping them after the fact. The detail band is the residual original − base. A noise floor σ is then estimated from the MAD (median absolute deviation) of that detail band, sampled on a grid, and every detail coefficient d is scaled by a Wiener-style gate d²/(d²+k²σ²): coefficients much larger than the noise floor (real texture, edges) pass close to full strength, while coefficients near the noise floor are suppressed. The Sharpen Mask slider sets k, i.e. how aggressively that gate protects grain, low values sharpen everything roughly evenly, high values leave flat areas such as skies and skin almost untouched while edges and texture get the full boost. Finally, the sharpened result is clamped to the local min/max of the original (plus a small allowance), a hard overshoot clamp that makes residual ringing physically impossible, regardless of amount or mask setting. All passes are separable, so cost stays linear in image size regardless of radius.

Lens distortion & vignetting

Distortion correction is a radial remap: each output pixel's normalised radius r from the image centre (0 at centre, 1 at the corners) is rescaled by a factor (1 + k·r²), and the source is bilinearly sampled at that adjusted radius, the standard division/Brown-Conrady form of radial-distortion modelling. For barrel correction (k>0) that pushes the sample radius past the source's own corners, so a complementary zoom S is solved for by Newton's method on S·(1 + k·S²) = 1, the point where the remapped corner lands exactly back on the source's edge, and applied before the remap, so the corrected image fills the frame with no transparent gaps. Pincushion correction (k<0) always samples strictly inside the source and needs no such compensation. Manual vignetting applies a smooth radial gain of (1 + a·r⁴), leaving the centre untouched and lifting or deepening the corners; the r⁴ falloff approximates the cos⁴ optical light-fall-off law. The EXIF-based suggestion is a name match, not a per-copy measurement: the file's LensModel tag (and, where the lens name alone is ambiguous, its camera Make tag) is matched against a small built-in reference table of typical Distortion/Vignetting values per lens model, so it is a sensible starting point to refine, not a calibrated correction.

Histogram & luminance

The histogram tallies all three channels in 256 bins over the preview, normalising to the tallest interior bin (the pure-black and pure-white endpoints are excluded so heavy clipping doesn’t flatten the curve). The optional luminance overlay uses the Rec. 601 luma weighting Y = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B. The clipping warning marks pixels where every channel is ≥254 (blown) or ≤1 (crushed), on a display-only copy so exported pixels are never altered.

Colour management

The sRGB and Display P3 ICC profiles are constructed at runtime from their defining primaries and tone-response curves, a real, spec-valid profile, not a guess. sRGB JPEGs are left untagged (sRGB is the universal default, so they render correctly everywhere), while Display P3 exports embed the P3 profile as an APP2 segment so colour-managed viewers reproduce the wide-gamut colours. HEIC/HEIF input uses the browser's native decoder where available and otherwise a WebAssembly HEIF decoder, with orientation baked into the pixels; AVIF and WebP decode natively.

Clone & patch

The clone tool records a source→target offset in normalised coordinates and replays it at export resolution. Before blending, it measures the mean colour difference between the source and target patches and applies a partial colour offset, so the copied texture carries over while the seam disappears under a feathered edge.

Workspace persistence

As you edit, the adjustment state and a cached working image are written to your browser's local IndexedDB store. Reopening the page restores the photo and every setting. Saves are throttled so dragging a slider stays smooth, and the data never leaves the device.

Subject detection

Detection combines a saliency/colour model with multi-scale edge operators and label propagation in CIELAB colour space. A brush stroke acts as a hard outer boundary so the mask refines to edges inside what you painted without leaking into a similar-coloured background. The five Detection sliders each control one stage of this pipeline:

Saliency: how distinct a pixel must be before it counts as subject. Raise it and only clearly-standout regions are selected, so the mask stays tight; lower it and more of the frame is pulled in. If you tapped a point on the subject, higher values also keep the grown selection closer to that tap.

Detail: how fine the traced edges are. High keeps hair, fur and small contours; low smooths past noise and follows only bold structural outlines. Raise it for wispy or intricate edges, lower it when surface texture is making the mask ragged.

Sensitivity: how faint an edge can be and still count as a boundary. High traces soft, low-contrast edges (useful for gentle transitions); low keeps only the strongest, cleanest contours. Lower it when faint background texture is being mistaken for edges.

BG Pinning: how tightly the mask hugs the area you brushed. High keeps the selection inside your strokes, which prevents leaks when the subject and background share a colour; low allows a little reach beyond the stroke for softer edges. Raise it whenever detection bleeds into the background.

Edge Snap: how strongly real contours block the fill from spreading. High makes the boundary snap hard to detected edges for a crisp cut; low gives a softer edge guided more by colour similarity than by contours. Raise it for clean, well-defined subjects and lower it for soft or fuzzy ones.

After changing any of these, tap Re-detect to re-run detection with the new settings.

Retouch tools

Heal searches nearby for a clean, low-variance donor patch, colour-matches it, and blends it over the target with a feathered edge, real texture, not blur. Smooth and Eyes use frequency separation: the image is split into low-frequency (colour) and high-frequency (pore) detail so softening or brightening can be applied while keeping texture.

Auto enhance

Auto samples a luma histogram and midtone colour means, then derives black/white points from robust percentiles (not raw min/max). It classifies the frame, aims the upper-midtone toward a sensible highlight target, applies grey-world white balance, and brakes every "punch" operation when the frame is already bright so highlights aren't blown.

Common issues

Retouch is not changing anything
Picking a tool (Heal/Smooth/Eyes) turns the brush on automatically; the button should read Retouch off, meaning it is currently active. Tap or drag directly on the photo. Increase Strength and Size if the effect is too subtle, and zoom in for precise work. Heal needs clean skin nearby to sample from; over a large flat area, try Smooth instead.
Editing feels slow on my device
While you drag a slider, the preview automatically renders at a reduced resolution matched to your device's speed, then snaps back to full quality the moment you let go, so sliders stay fluid even on modest phones, and nothing about the exported file changes. Heavy effects (sharpening, clarity, grain, denoise) are also deferred to the moment you release. If it still feels sluggish, close other heavy tabs, since everything runs on your device.
Why does the histogram look spiky or discontinuous after editing?
The histogram is read from the 8-bit preview buffer that is drawn to the screen; the canvas can only display 8-bit, so that is what the on-screen histogram measures. Edits like curves, contrast, HSL and presets remap those 256 display levels; stretching part of the tonal range spreads a few input levels across more output values, leaving gaps between "teeth" while other values pile into spikes. That combing is a normal side-effect of visualising remapped 8-bit data, and stacking several strong adjustments makes it more visible. It does not mean your photo is banding: for a RAW, tone and curves are actually applied to the 16-bit sensor master through a 65,536-entry LUT, and JPEG/PNG/TIFF exports tone-map from that master, so the exported file carries far more tonal precision than the preview histogram's 256 bins can show. The spikes are in the 8-bit readout, not in your rendered result.
A preset looks too strong
Every preset now has a Preset strength slider just below the thumbnails; 100% is the full look, lower values blend it toward your original. All values stay editable afterwards.
Where do I start as a beginner?
Open a photo and look at the Photo Assistant at the top of the Quick tab; it measures the photo and suggests one-tap fixes in plain language, each with a short reason. Apply what sounds right (everything is reversible), hold the eye button to compare with the original, then try a preset. The Insights tab explains what your photo does well and what to try next time you shoot.
Auto enhance looks too strong
Lower the Auto intensity in the action-bar Auto menu, or fine-tune individual sliders afterward. Auto only sets a starting point; every value remains editable. You can also tap the applied Auto enhance row in the Photo Assistant to undo it entirely.
The screen asks me to rotate my phone
Landscape editing is not supported on phones, since the screen is too short to show both the photo and the editing sheet, so the app asks you to rotate back to portrait. Tablets and laptops can use landscape normally.
Auto picked the wrong orientation
Open the Auto menu and choose Portrait or Landscape explicitly instead of Auto, then re-run.
Subject detection leaks into the background
Brush over the subject so detection is confined to your strokes, then raise BG Pinning and Edge Snap. When subject and background share a colour, paint out to the rim and use the mask touch-up brush to clean edges.
Which RAW formats are fully supported?
Mainstream RAW files get a full decode, either by reconstructing the sensor data (demosaicing) or reading the camera's full-size embedded preview: ARW (Sony), NEF (Nikon), CR2/CR3 (Canon), DNG, ORF (Olympus), RW2 (Panasonic) and RAF (Fuji). Rarer formats, PEF, SRW, 3FR, X3F, IIQ, MEF, MRW, KDC, DCR and similar, are opened on a best-effort, embedded-preview basis: if the camera stored a usable JPEG preview it opens fine, otherwise it may not load. These are shown with a dashed outline on the welcome screen. When a file cannot be read either way, you will get a clear message rather than a silent failure.
A RAW file will not open
NijRAW reads the raw sensor data or the embedded JPEG preview inside RAW files. A few cameras, more often the rarer, preview-only formats above, omit a usable preview; try exporting a JPEG/TIFF from your camera software, or convert to DNG, which always opens.
A large RAW takes a while to open
Sensor-data RAWs are unpacked and demosaiced in the background using WebAssembly in a worker, so the app stays responsive while a big file decodes. Files that take longest are usually very large sensor frames; the embedded-preview path is faster when a camera provides one.
Denoise preview seems delayed
Denoising runs off the main thread, so the denoised preview appears a moment after you release the slider rather than instantly, and this keeps the interface from freezing. Full-resolution denoise is pre-computed in the background once you settle the slider and cached, so export normally does not have to wait for it; if it does run at export time, a progress message is shown.
Export is slow or the tab feels heavy
Full-resolution export processes every pixel and can take a moment on very large files. With Denoise active, the full-size pass now starts quietly in the background a couple of seconds after you settle the slider, and the finished result is remembered, so exporting (and re-exporting in another format) is usually near-instant. If you export immediately after changing Denoise, the pass runs during export with a progress bar. Close other heavy tabs if your device is low on memory.
A HEIC photo will not open
HEIC/HEIF photos from modern phones open on every browser. Where the browser cannot decode them natively (most Chrome and Firefox versions), NijRAW uses a built-in WebAssembly HEIF decoder that is part of the app, so it works fully offline, with nothing uploaded. A large HEIC may take a moment to decode. If a specific file still fails it may use an unusual variant; converting it to JPEG will always work. AVIF and WebP open everywhere too.
WebP or AVIF export buttons are not showing
Those buttons only appear when your browser can encode that format. If you do not see them, your browser does not support that encoder; use JPEG or PNG instead.
What is a .nijraw file, and how do I save one?
It is NijRAW's own project format: your untouched original photo plus every edit, mask and adjustment in one file. Tap Export → Save project (.nijraw) to write it to your device. Later, tap Import (or drag the file in) and pick that .nijraw file to reopen it exactly as you left it and keep editing; unlike a JPEG/PNG/TIFF export, nothing is baked in.
How do I export without EXIF/GPS metadata?
Uncheck Include metadata in the export popover before tapping a format button. With it off, camera details (make, model, lens, ISO, capture time) and any GPS location are left out of the JPEG, WebP or TIFF file. It is unchecked or checked per export, so set it each time you export if you want it to differ from your last export.
My shared recipe does not include the LUT
A recipe stores your adjustments plus the LUT's name and intensity, but not the LUT file itself (that would bloat the JSON). To reproduce the look exactly, load the same .cube file, then apply the recipe; the intensity will match.
A local mask is not doing anything
Make sure the mask is selected in the list and at least one of its sliders is moved off zero; an empty mask has no effect (the editor shows a warning while all sliders are at zero). Check Strength is not at 0%. For radial masks, check the Feather and that the shape covers the area; for brush masks, paint over the region you want. Hidden masks are skipped; tap the eye icon on the row to show them again.
Clone is not copying anything
The first tap only sets the source point; you will see a "Source set" note. Paint after that to copy from it. Tap Set new source to choose a different area to copy from.
Colours look different in another app
Export as JPEG with the sRGB colour profile for the most consistent results across apps and the web. Use Display P3 only when the destination is known to be wide-gamut; on a non-managed viewer P3 files can look oversaturated.
My edits disappeared
Use Undo (Ctrl/⌘+Z), or open the History panel and click an earlier step. Your session is also saved in your browser as you work, so refreshing or reopening the page restores the photo and settings. Choosing New session (closing the photo) clears that saved workspace. Nothing is ever stored remotely.
NijRAW
Runs entirely on your device
  • A Photo editor that develops, retouches and exports your photos right here in the browser.
  • Your photos and their data never leave this device, nothing is uploaded.
  • To start: load a photo, tap Auto for a one-tap improvement, then explore the panels.

The demo opens on YouTube in a new browser tab. Everything else in NijRAW stays on your device, and nothing is uploaded.

Checked means you will never see this again. Left unchecked, tapping Get started closes it for now but shows it again next launch. You can always reopen it from Help → Show welcome screen.
Please rotate your phone
Landscape editing is not supported on phones. Turn your device back to portrait to continue. Tablets and laptops can use landscape as usual.
